human_tolerance.notes: Roosts in mines, caves, tunnels, buildings, bat boxes, tree cavities, storm drains, wood piles and rock crevices, and forages in cities around street lamps; its tolerance of habitat modification by humans is one of the reasons the IUCN lists it as least concern.

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: 'Big brown bats enter into hibernation around November ... in a location less than 80 km away from their summer roosts' and 'come out of hibernation in the spring.' The day boundaries are the author's judgement, as the article gives only 'around November' and 'in the spring'.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: 'Their breeding season is in the fall, shortly before their annual hibernation' and 'Big brown bat mating season is in the fall.' The window is the author's judgement around the stated season.

phases.name: young
phases.note: 'After hibernation ends in the spring, females form maternity colonies for giving birth to young', with 'pregnant females separate into maternity colonies around April' and, in the eastern United States, 'twins are commonly born sometime between May and July'.

vocalizations.description: The ultrasonic echolocation call the species emits into its environment and listens to the returning echoes of. From it the bat works out how far away an object is, the object's size, shape and density, and the direction in which anything is moving; the buzz is continuous while foraging and is not audible to a human observer.

taxonomy.note: Beauvois 1806, Eptesicus fuscus - 'It was first described as a species in 1796'; family Vespertilionidae per the GBIF backbone and ITIS TSN 180008.

common_names.note: en/fr/es labels; the English name follows the Wikipedia article title, the fr/es labels the Wikidata sitelink titles.

conservation.note: 'The big brown bat is not considered at risk for extinction, and is evaluated as the lowest conservation priority by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).' Wikidata P141 also gives LC (Q211005).

range.note: From the lead: 'distributed widely throughout North America, the Caribbean, and the northern portion of South America', and 'occurs widely throughout the US, Canada, Central America, and the Caribbean. Its range extends into parts of South America, found as far south as Colombia and Venezuela.' Koppen classes are the author's judgement of the described range.

traits.body_plan.note: Vertebrate, chordate, four-limbed, furred, endothermic mammal with a membrane wing on each forelimb; traits.body_plan records the vertebrate plan the schema uses, and the mesh's body plan is noted under `look`.

traits.limb_count.note: Four: the forelimbs are modified into wings, as in every bat, and the two hind limbs are separate and very short - 'the hind legs are 10 millimetres'.

traits.locomotion_modes.note: Powered flight, plus climbing to reach a roost: the article describes a species that 'will utilize a wide variety of structures for roosts' including 'tree cavities' and 'under exfoliating bark', and bats climb rather than fly the last stretch into a cavity.

traits.thermoregulation.note: Endotherm: a mammal that is 'relatively resistant to the effects of [white-nose syndrome]' and uses 'large deposits of brown fat, which provides the bats with a source of energy to rapidly increase body temperature upon arousal from hibernation'.

traits.skin.note: Fur: 'Its dorsal fur is reddish brown and glossy in appearance; its ventral fur is lighter brown. Its snout, uropatagium (flight membrane between the hind limbs), and wing membranes are black and hairless.'

traits.flight.note: Powered flight: 'the species emits a call out into its environment and listens to the echoes of those calls that return from various objects near them' to navigate, and it forages in the air around street lamps.

traits.respiration.note: Lungs: a mammalian respiratory system, the lungs having to serve the high metabolic demand of echolocation and flight.

traits.metamorphosis.note: None: 'At birth, pups are blind, helpless, and only 3 g ... The pup nurses from its mother for approximately one month. Pups fledge, or begin flying, at three to five weeks old.'

traits.nest_type.note: Gives birth and raises young in a roost, not a nest: a cavity in a cave, mine, tunnel, tree, building or bat box. The schema's Cavity value is the closest fit for that site.

traits.perching.note: False: bats hang from a roost and cling to its ceiling rather than perching on a branch, so the schema's perching flag, which describes a bird on a branch, does not apply.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg: the validator bands an animal under 0.05 kg as Tiny, and 0.021 kg is well inside that band.

traits.length_m.note: Midpoint of 'Adult body length is 110-130 mm (4.3-5.1 in)' (head and body, excluding the wings).

traits.wingspan_m.note: Midpoint of 'possessing a wingspan of 32.5-35 cm (12.8-13.8 in)'.

traits.diet.note: 'Big brown bats are insectivorous, consuming a diverse array of insects, particularly night-flying insects, but especially beetles', and 'it is generally considered a beetle specialist', with beetles 'present in 99.2% of fecal samples' in an Ontario study. The whole diet is the single insect share.

traits.social.note: 'Maternity colonies range in size from 5-700 individuals, though in the eastern US and Canada, they are frequently 25-75 adults'; males are solitary or in 'small, all-male colonies', and 'Females exhibit philopatry' with '10-30% of female offspring returning to their natal roost'. Group with a range up to a typical eastern maternity colony is used; the 700-bird maximum is a documented outlier.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'The big brown bat is nocturnal, roosting in sheltered places during the day' and 'foraging for prey at night'.

traits.defense.note: Authored: 'The big brown bat has few natural predators. Predation occurs opportunistically' by grackles, kestrels, owls, weasels and bullfrogs, with no defensive display of its own, so fleeing by flight is the closest schema value.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: it roosts 'in buildings ... thus have a higher chance of encountering humans' and is 'often found in proximity to humans', which is tolerance rather than wariness, tempered by its dependence on dark secluded roosts and its start at a hand approaching the roost.

habitat.use.note: 'Their use of echolocation allows them to occupy a niche where there are often many insects (that come out at night since there are fewer predators then)' and it 'will forage in cities around street lamps', so the animal spends the night in the air; the arboreal share is climbing to and clinging in its roost.

habitat.shelter_tag.note: 'They will utilize a wide variety of structures for roosts, including mines, caves, tunnels, buildings, bat boxes, tree cavities, storm drains, wood piles, and rock crevicles ... They generally roost in cavities.'

habitat.resources.note: The whole diet is the one invertebrate resource, weighted at 1.0; cavity is both the roost and the maternity site, and perch covers clinging to the roost ceiling.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: urban_affinity and uses_gardens from 'It is adaptable to many habitats and is considered a generalist species', from roosting in 'buildings, bat boxes' and wood piles, and from foraging 'in cities around street lamps'; the article also lists 'tolerance to habitat modification by humans' as one of the IUCN criteria it meets. light_max, flight_distance_m and road_mortality are judgement values, the article giving no figures.

seasonal.strategy.note: Hibernation: 'Big brown bats enter into hibernation around November, often in a location less than 80 km away from their summer roosts' and 'Big brown bats come out of hibernation in the spring.'

seasonal.phases.note: The article gives the sequence and the months only in outline: 'Their breeding season is in the fall, shortly before their annual hibernation', 'enter into hibernation around November', 'come out of hibernation in the spring', 'After hibernation ends in the spring, females form maternity colonies for giving birth to young', 'around April', and 'twins are commonly born sometime between May and July' in the eastern United States. The phase windows are the author's judgement, placed on those months; the eastern-US birth window is the one that applies to Arkansas.

seasonal.life_stages.note: 'The pup nurses from its mother for approximately one month ... Pups fledge, or begin flying, at three to five weeks old.' duration_days is the age at fledging, and scale is a judgement of a newly flying pup against its mother's body mass.

seasonal.triggers.note: The schema requires weather triggers for Hibernation. The article gives no temperature, only that bats 'tolerate cold weather fairly well' and 'can be negatively affected by major changes in temperature', and that the colony hibernates 'in warm man-made structures'. 10 C over five days is authored as a plausible autumn threshold for a species that hibernates in buildings rather than in cold caves; it is a stated estimate, not a sourced figure, and the exit trigger uses the same threshold rising, following the existing erinaceus-europaeus record's convention.

look.note: Coat and membranes from the Description section: 'Its dorsal fur is reddish brown and glossy in appearance; its ventral fur is lighter brown. Its snout, uropatagium (flight membrane between the hind limbs), and wing membranes are black and hairless.' Proportions are judgement, with a short rounded snout and a low wing aspect ratio for the broad rounded wings a vesper bat flies with; the tail_membrane part carries the black uropatagium. The wing parts are held at the dark membrane colour rather than the fur colour, because the article says the wing membranes are black and hairless while only the body and head carry fur - without that the model reads as one solid brown plank. The mesh uses the kit's biped_winged plan, the only one with wings, and the record says so rather than pretending a bat is a bird.

behavior.note: Authored parameters, and the closest of the four shared programs. No shared program is a bat, but fsm-ground-forager-v1 is parameterised by gait: both flee_gait and forage_gait are set to fly, which is the only change needed to make its idle/wander/forage/drink/flee/rest cycle run in the air, and its default rest window of 10-90 degrees of sun elevation is the daytime rest its own description documents as correct 'for nocturnal and crepuscular species' - a bat roosting by day. A bespoke program would duplicate the whole state machine to change two gait strings, so none was written; the one gap is that the program's forage acts on the nearest tagged resource in reach, where a bat actually detects insects by echolocation in the open air.
